## 4. lore — why laama and kudunga aren't single words

**ANNA:** why laama and kudunga aren't single words

**ANNA:** polama isn't one word, it's grammar hiding inside a suffix, an entire permission request bolted onto a verb.

**ANNA:** -லாமா
> the laam part means can or may, tack it onto any verb stem and you're stating a possibility.

**ANNA:** add the question tone at the end and it flips from a statement into asking, that shift alone turns can into may I.

**ANNA:** குடுங்க
> kudunga looks like just give plus manners, but kongu speakers actually shift the vowel first, kodu becomes kudu before the polite tail ever gets added.

**ANNA:** கொடு
> that's the dictionary root, give, say it slow and you can hear where kudu came from.

**ANNA:** the -nga on the end does two jobs at once, plural and respectful, same tag you'd use with your maama or a shopkeeper you just met.

**ANNA:** so kudunga is really three pieces welded together, give, you, and polite, and a coimbatore ear hears all three without ever noticing the seams.

## 10. lore — The word behind "can't" — முடி

**ANNA:** The word behind "can't" — முடி

**ANNA:** முடி
> here's a thing nobody tells you about the can't word, முடியல் — its root is முடி, and that root does triple duty in Tamil.

**ANNA:** முடி means hair. it also means to finish, to complete something.

**ANNA:** so when you say you can't lift something, you're not saying 'I lack the strength'.

**ANNA:** தூக்க முடியல
> you're literally saying the finishing doesn't happen — தூக்க முடியல means the lifting never completes.

**ANNA:** ability in Tamil isn't your personal power, it's whether the task reaches its end.

**ANNA:** that's why there's no real subject doing the failing in that sentence — the task itself just doesn't finish.

**ANNA:** முடிவு
> same root gives you முடிவு — an ending, a decision, a conclusion.

**ANNA:** so next time you say முடியல், you're borrowing the same word an auntie uses for tying up her hair.
